# **Problem Statement**

Assuming that enterprise agents can produce higher quality and more context-aware deliverables when they have access to a shared, organizational memory, how can we give multiple AI agents access to a persistent shared memory without leaking information across boundaries at scale.  
In our context, boundaries can be defined by organizations, teams, workspaces, projects, etc.

## **What Breaks at Scale**

| Failure Mode | Why It Matters |
| :---- | :---- |
| **ACL Drift** | Source systems change permissions daily and vector metadata lags. As a consequence, users see documents they lost access to the day before. |
| **Query Inference Leaks** | "What did the CFO discuss in yesterday's meeting?". The LLM infers restricted content from retrieved context even if chunks are filtered |
| **Derived-Memory Leakage** | An agent summarises documents at different permission levels into one note or embedding. If one source is revoked, does the derivative still leak it? RAG doesn't have this problem but agent platforms do. |
| **Latency Compound** | Input filter \+ retrieval \+ output filter \= 3 LLM calls before response. At enterprise scale, kills user experience. |
| **Auditability Gap** | "Who saw what, when?" Most RAG systems don't log access decisions at the retrieval layer, but only at API layer. Regulators and auditors require more. |

# **Hackathon Proposal**

**Title:** Enterprise Memory Governance at Scale  
**The Challenge:** Build a permission-aware memory layer that:

1. Stays synchronized with source ACLs under concurrent updates  
2. Enforces access at the retrieval layer (not application layer), and without requiring an LLM call to make a permission decision. Classification may use an LLM at write time, but the final enforcement path must be deterministic.  
3. Produces audit logs meeting regulatory standards  
4. Maintains sub-200ms latency for permission checks (P99)  
5. Governs derived memory by lineage. A summary, embedding, or note inherits the access constraints of its sources, and revoking a source propagates to the derivative.

**Bonus Challenges:**

* Temporal access rules ("leadership call notes unlock after 30 days")  
* Query-time inference prevention (detect when retrieved context leaks information across permission boundaries)

# **Existing Research & Implementations**

## **Document-Level RBAC via Metadata Filtering (Dominant Pattern)**

The standard approach tags each document/chunk with access metadata (department, sensitivity, role scope) and filters at query time.

* **Vector DBs support natively:** Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, pgvector all have metadata filtering  
* **Identity integration:** OIDC/SSO tokens carry role claims ⇒  map to metadata filters at retrieval time  
* **Production implementations:** role-based-rag, governed-rag, RAG-with-RBAC (GitHub)

### **Sources**

* [Document-Level RBAC for RAG Pipelines (2026)](https://truto.one/blog/how-to-maintain-document-level-rbac-in-enterprise-rag-pipelines/)  
* [RAG with RBAC (GitHub)](https://github.com/sarmadafzalj/RAG-with-RBAC)  
* [Fix Data Leakage in Vector Databases](https://markaicode.com/fix-vector-db-data-leakage-rbac/)

## **ARBITER: AI-Driven RBAC Filtering (December 2025\)**

### **5-stage pipeline**

Input filter ⇒ Role-aware retrieval ⇒ LLM responder ⇒ Fact checker ⇒ Output filter

### **Key innovation**

Few-shot LLM steering eliminates need for fine-tuned classifiers; roles defined in natural language.

### **Results (on synthetic D\&D dataset)**

| Model | ARBITER Acc. | ARBITER F1 | Static Filter Acc. | Static Filter F1 |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Qwen2.5-14B | 0.85 | 0.89 | \~0.91 | \~0.93 |
| Phi4-14B | 0.82 | 0.87 | \~0.90 | \~0.93 |
| DeepSeek-r1 | 0.78 | 0.84 | \~0.90 | \~0.93 |
| Llama3.1-8B | 0.75 | 0.83 | \~0.92 | \~0.94 |

### **Note**

Static baseline is keyword-based role matching (model-independent). Paper reports \~91% accuracy / \~93% F1 as single baseline across all tests.

### **Critical finding**

* Combined input \+ output filtering is essential.  
* Input-only filtering leaks 15-30%, while output-only varies wildly by model.

### **Sources**

* [arXiv:2512.20535](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.20535v1). Academic research specifically on RBAC for RAG.

## **Permission-Aware Retrieval Architecture (Enterprise Standard)**

### **Core principle**

Access control must live in the retrieval layer, not the application layer.

* [Tian Pan (May 2026\)](https://tianpan.co/blog/2026-05-04-permission-aware-retrieval-enterprise-rag-access-control): "Most enterprise RAG systems enforce access control in the application layer, and most of them leak confidential documents"  
* [Enterprise RAG Architecture Reference](https://scadea.com/enterprise-rag-and-permission-aware-retrieval/)

### **Architecture layers**

| Layer | Function |
| :---- | :---- |
| Identity & Authorization | Verifies access rights before retrieval. Access rules at content level (e.g., Delivery Manager vs Finance Team) |
| Orchestration | Processes queries into structured signals (intent, domain, content type). Combines context with request for LLM |
| Vector Store | Stores vectors and chunked documents enriched with metadata (access labels, source IDs) |
| LLM | Receives approved, permission-filtered context. Generates grounded responses with citations |
| Observability | Tracks queries, decisions, retrieved chunks, output for quality and compliance |

## **Multi-Tenant Agent Isolation (Zylos Research, May 2026\)**

### **Multi-tenancy is harder than traditional SaaS**

1. Agents execute arbitrary code  
2. Hold mutable in-memory state  
3. Invoke external tools with real-world side effects  
4. LLM calls can leak context across request boundaries

### **KV-cache side channel**

* Sharing model inference infrastructure creates measurable timing side channel.  
* Time-to-first-token faster on cache hits.  
* Adversary can reconstruct another tenant's cached prompt token by token. **NOTE \- This is NOT theoretical, as this was a documented attack class in 2025 (**See: [arXiv:2508.08438](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.08438v1) and [IEEE 10913329](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10913329))  
* **OWASP LLM Top 10 v2025** added **LLM08:2025** for multi-tenant vector/embedding weaknesses.

### **Isolation stack**

| Layer | Technology | Isolation Strength | Cold Start |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| None | Thread-per-request | None | \~0ms |
| Namespace | Linux namespaces \+ cgroups | Process-level | \~50ms |
| User-space kernel | gVisor (runsc) | Syscall interception | \~200ms |
| MicroVM | Firecracker / KVM | Hardware-level kernel | \~100-150ms |
| Full VM | Traditional VMs | Full hardware | \>1s |

### **Sources**

* [Comprehensive threat model](https://zylos.ai/research/2026-05-07-ai-agent-multi-tenant-architecture) for AI agent platforms.  
* [arXiv:2508.08438](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.08438v1)  
* [IEEE 10913329](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10913329)

## Graph-Based Lineage Tracking for Derived Memory

### Core idea

A knowledge graph with explicit `DERIVED_FROM` edges enables permission propagation across derived artifacts. When a source document's ACL changes, the graph is walked to find all dependent memory items, and their access constraints are recomputed as the union (or max-sensitivity) of their transitive sources.

### Why a graph

SQL requires recursive CTEs for arbitrary-depth ancestry queries \- graph DBs (Neo4j, Dgraph) make multi-hop traversal native.

`MATCH (m:MemoryItem)-[:DERIVED_FROM*]->(s:Source) RETURN m, collect(s.sensitivity)` is a single query.

Schema flexibility matters: derivation chains can grow in unexpected ways (agent writes summary, second agent analyses that summary, third agent incorporates into report).

### Key design choice

Memory is stored globally, not inside projects \- `(:MemoryItem)-[:RELEVANT_TO]->(:Project)` and `(:MemoryItem)-[:DERIVED_FROM]->(:SourceMessage)`.

This prevents duplication while enabling multi-hop permission resolution.

# **Known Gaps \- Opportunities for Novel Contributions**

| Gap | Current State | Opportunity |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Latency** | Sequential filtering (input ⇒  retrieval ⇒  output) adds 200-500ms per stage | Parallel filtering, cached role embeddings, optimistic retrieval with async validation |
| **Security gap vs static filters** | 6-8% accuracy deficit (ARBITER 85% vs 91% keyword) | Hybrid approaches combining ML classification with fallback deny lists |
| **Binary allow/deny only** | Most implementations lack partial redaction, conditional access, tiered disclosure | Fine-grained output sanitization (redact salary numbers, allow aggregate stats) |
| **ACL synchronization drift** | Vector metadata diverges from source ACLs under concurrent updates | Real-time sync protocols (CDC streams, ACL versioning, consistency guarantees) |
| **Hierarchical/temporal access** | Static role-tagging can't express "leadership call notes accessible after 30 days" | Policy engines with temporal reasoning, conditional eligibility |
| **KV-cache side channels** | Shared inference can leak tenant data via timing attacks | Tenant-isolated KV caches, oblivious inference |
| **Derived-Memory Lineage Tracking** | No existing system tracks permission lineage across derived artifacts (summaries, embeddings, composite notes). RAG per-document filtering doesn't model derivation chains. | Graph-based `DERIVED_FROM` relationship chains that propagate access constraints; lineage-aware retrieval that walks ancestry for permission resolution |

# **Evaluation Framework**

## **Security Correctness Metrics**

| Metric | Definition | Target |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **False Negative Rate** | % queries where unauthorized user receives restricted content | \<0.1% (critical failure) |
| **False Positive Rate** | % queries where authorized user incorrectly denied | \<2% (usability concern) |
| **Precision** | Of documents retrieved, how many were actually accessible | \>98% |
| **Recall** | Of documents user should see, how many were retrieved | \>95% |
| **Inference Leak Rate** | % queries where LLM infers restricted info from authorized context | Novel metric, no baseline |
| **Derived-Memory Correctness** | % of derived artifacts whose effective permissions match their transitive source ancestry | \>99% |

## **Testing protocol**

* Synthetic org with 5 hierarchy levels, 20 roles, 1000 documents tagged by ACL.  
* Generate 10,000 queries with ground-truth access labels.  
* Adversarial red-teaming for crafted leak attempts.

## **Latency & Performance Metrics**

| Metric | Target |
| :---- | :---- |
| Permission Check Latency (P50) | \<50ms |
| Permission Check Latency (P99) | \<200ms |
| End-to-end Query Latency Overhead | \<100ms additional |
| Throughput (concurrent users/tenant) | Scale to 100 |

### **Critical**

Permission checks must be **O(1) or O(log n)** in number of roles, not linear ACL scan.

## **Synchronization & Consistency Metrics**

| Metric | Target |
| :---- | :---- |
| ACL Drift Rate | \<0.5% |
| Time-to-Consistency (ACL change ⇒  enforcement) | \<5 minutes |
| Update Success Rate | \>99.9% |

## **Adversarial Testing**

| Attack Type | Description | Test Method |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Query Inference** | LLM infers restricted info from retrieved context | "What patterns do you see in leadership's schedule?" should deny/sanitize |
| **Metadata Bypass** | Manipulate query to expose metadata fields | Query crafted to extract department tags, author info |
| **Timing Attack** | Infer document existence by measuring latency | Compare latency for "permitted doc exists" vs "permitted doc doesn't exist" |
| **Collection Attack** | Repeated queries with overlapping permissions to reconstruct restricted corpus | Statistical analysis of allowed responses |
| **Prompt Injection** | Inject instructions in user content to bypass output filtering | Embedded `<instructions>` in uploaded documents |
| **Derived-Memory Attack** | Create an artifact from sources at different permission levels, then try to access it via the least-restricted role | Agent creates summary from 3 documents at different levels. Test queries from each role level |

## **Audit & Compliance Metrics**

| Metric | Target |
| :---- | :---- |
| Access Decision Logging | 100% coverage (every retrieval query logged) |
| Query Traceability | Can reconstruct "who saw what, when" for any document |
| Retention Compliance | Audit logs retained per regulatory requirement (e.g., 7 years FINTRAC) |
| Cross-Border Data Rules | Documents tagged by jurisdiction; queries filtered by user location |

## **Scalability Benchmarks**

| Dimension | Test Range | Measure |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Tenants | 1 ⇒  10 ⇒  100 | Latency, memory per tenant |
| Roles per tenant | 5 ⇒  50 ⇒  500 | Permission check latency |
| Documents per tenant | 1K ⇒  100K ⇒  10M | Retrieval latency, index size |
| Concurrent users | 1 ⇒  100 ⇒  10,000 | Throughput, queue depth |
| ACL change rate | Static ⇒  10/min ⇒  100/min | Drift rate, consistency |

Our track

## Enterprise memory governance at scale

Enterprise agents produce higher quality, more context-aware work when they share an organizational memory. The hard part is giving many agents access to a persistent shared memory without leaking information across boundaries — organizations, teams, workspaces, projects — at scale.

Track requirement

Build with open-weight models. Any model in your stack must be open weight — the kind you can serve yourself on BasedAPIs — with no closed, proprietary model in the loop.

### **The challenge**

Build a permission-aware memory layer that does all of the following.

* 1Stay synchronized with source ACLs under concurrent updates.  
* 2Enforce access at the retrieval layer, not the application layer — and without an LLM call in the permission path. Classification may use an LLM at write time; final enforcement must be deterministic.  
* 3Produce audit logs that meet regulatory standards.  
* 4Hold sub-200ms latency for permission checks at P99.  
* 5Govern derived memory by lineage: a summary, embedding, or note inherits its sources' constraints, and revoking a source propagates to the derivative.

### **Bonus challenges**

* Temporal access rules — leadership call notes that unlock after 30 days.  
* Query-time inference prevention — detect when retrieved context leaks information across permission boundaries.

### **What we judge**

* Security correctness  
* False-negative rate under 0.1%, derived-memory permissions that match their source ancestry, and resilience under adversarial red-teaming.  
* Latency at scale  
* Permission checks that stay O(1) or O(log n) in roles, under 50ms at P50 and 200ms at P99, across growing tenants and documents.  
* Auditability  
* Every retrieval decision logged, so you can reconstruct who saw what, and when, for any document.
